events.text: A herald nails a notice to the town gate: the provincial rounds of the Heavenly Tournament, open to all comers, three days from now. A crowd forms around the notice, and every second person in it is stretching.

ok.log: You win four bouts in three days and your name goes up on the board in red ink. People point at you in the street.

fail.log: You lose in the third bout to someone who bows very politely afterwards. The crowd claps for you anyway.

choices.text: Watch from the stands and study

effects.log: You watch a hundred bouts and fill a notebook with what you saw. Three of the pages are worth a year of training.
The crowd is thirsty and you are quick. By the end of the rounds your purse is heavier.

events.text: Between the rounds of the Heavenly Tournament a young fighter in a borrowed robe stops you in the practice yard. "They say you are good," the fighter says. "I would like to know before the stage does."

ok.log: It is a good spar, the kind you remember. You both walk away grinning, and the fighter tells everyone who won.

fail.log: The fighter is better than the robe. You lose, laughing, and come away with a new idea about footwork.

effects.log: You eat noodles on the steps and talk about masters and roads. You make a friend for the length of a festival.
You bow and walk on. Somewhere behind you the fighter finds someone else to test.

events.text: The last day of the Heavenly Tournament. Ten thousand people pack the stands around the great stage, and two masters you have only heard of salute each other under the banners.

choices.text: Find a seat close to the stage

effects.log: You see every move from twenty paces. When the winner raises a hand, you are close enough to see it shake.

choices.text: Help the physicians behind the stage

effects.log: You carry water and hold bandages for the beaten. One of them, a famous name, thanks you by name.

choices.text: Skip it and train while the town is empty

effects.log: The practice yards are yours alone all day. The roar of the stands comes over the roofs like weather.

events.text: A column of refugees comes down the western road, carts piled high, children asleep on bundles. Behind them, very far off, smoke stands up from the passes where the Demon Tide has broken through.

choices.text: Escort them to the next town

ok.log: Raiders come out of the dusk on the second night. You send them back into it. The column reaches the walls whole.

fail.log: The raiders get two carts before you drive them off. Everyone lives. You carry a wound and a grudge.

effects.log: A cart of rice and fifty taels. An old man tries to give you his only knife in thanks; you will not take it.

choices.text: Point them to the river road

effects.log: They take the river road. You do not hear of them again, which is the best news there is.

events.text: The orthodox sects hold the Iron Gate Pass against the Demon Tide. Their call for volunteers is nailed to every inn door: anyone who can hold a weapon, for one night on the wall.

choices.text: Stand one night on the wall

ok.log: The black banners come three times in the night and three times go back down the slope. At dawn an elder writes down your name.

fail.log: You are carried off the wall before midnight, but the wall holds, and your name is on the list of those who stood.

effects.log: You run arrows up the stairs until your legs stop working. Nobody notices you, and the wall holds.
You listen to the drums from three valleys away and do not sleep much.

events.text: In a teahouse a traveller asks too many questions about the sects' supply roads. The traveller's sleeve rides up for a moment, and there is a black flame tattooed on the wrist.

ok.log: You follow the black flame to a mill outside town and bring the sect guards back with you. The supply road is safe for a season.

fail.log: You lose the traveller in the market. You report it anyway, and the guards double the watch.

choices.text: Tell the sect guards at once

effects.log: The guards take it seriously. By evening the traveller is gone, and so are the questions.
You finish your tea. Some things are not your business, until they are.

events.text: Pilgrims fill the mountain road to the old temple, a long line of straw hats and prayer beads. An old pilgrim has sat down by the road and cannot get up again.

choices.text: Carry the old pilgrim to the temple

effects.log: It takes all afternoon. At the top the old pilgrim weeps, and the monks give you a bowl of rice and a blessing.
You walk the last thousand steps with the pilgrims. At the top the wind is very clean.

choices.text: Sell straw sandals to the pilgrims

effects.log: Your sandals sell out by noon. Somebody blesses you anyway.

events.text: On the night of the pilgrims' festival a thousand lamps are lit on the temple steps, one for every prayer. A monk holds an unlit lamp out to you.

choices.text: Light it with a prayer for the dead

effects.log: You light it for everyone you have lost. The flame stands very straight.

choices.text: Light it with a prayer for yourself

effects.log: You ask for one thing, and you do not tell anyone what it was.

choices.text: Give it to a child with no lamp

effects.log: The child lights it with both hands and runs off to show someone. The monk smiles at you.

events.text: A wandering monk on the pilgrim road carries a bone relic in a wooden box and asks for help: there are bandits on the pass ahead, and the relic must reach the temple before the festival ends.

choices.text: Guard the monk over the pass

ok.log: The bandits take one look at you and decide to rob someone else. The relic reaches the temple on the last day.

fail.log: The bandits take your silver and leave the box, which they think is empty. The monk thanks you very much.

choices.text: Show the monk a hidden path

effects.log: You know a goat track around the pass. The monk goes over it with the box on a back and a prayer on the lips.
The monk bows and goes on alone. You hope the bandits are asleep.

events.text: Far away in {pw_world}, {pw_people} walk to your temples for their great festival. You feel it as a warmth, thousands of small voices saying the same name at once: yours.

choices.text: Answer with a sign in the sky

effects.log: A ring of light over every temple at once. In {pw_world} they will tell of it for a hundred years.
You listen all night. Most of them ask for rain, or for a child to get well. You remember them.

choices.text: Stay silent and let them keep it their own way

effects.log: They keep it without you, and that is a kind of faith too.

events.text: In {pw_world} a single pilgrim has walked for a whole year to your oldest temple, barefoot, carrying nothing but a question. The question is for you.

choices.text: Appear to the pilgrim in a dream

effects.log: You answer in a dream. The pilgrim wakes and walks home, and the answer is told in every village on the way.
The pilgrim comes home to fields heavier than they have ever been, and understands.

choices.text: Let the long walk be the answer

effects.log: The pilgrim sits at the temple door until dawn and then smiles, as if something was said.

events.text: The priests of {pw_world} want to raise a new temple on the road the pilgrims walk, and they argue about where: by the river, or on the mountain where you first stood.

effects.log: They build it by the river, and travellers stop there to drink and pray. It is never empty.
They build it on the mountain, and the climb becomes part of the prayer. The faithful get very strong legs.
Two temples in one season. The priests are exhausted and very happy.

events.text: The Hundred-Pill Fair fills the market town with furnaces. An alchemist with singed eyebrows offers a pill that "opens every meridian in one night", for 80 taels.

effects.log: It tastes of chalk and honey and opens nothing. You feel very healthy, though, for a week.

ok.log: Chalk, honey and a pinch of ginseng. You tell the alchemist so, loudly, and the crowd laughs the alchemist out of town.

fail.log: You cannot tell what is in it. You do not buy it, which is wisdom of a kind.

choices.text: Walk on and look at the real masters

effects.log: You watch an old alchemist turn a furnace with bare hands and learn more than any pill could teach.

events.text: The fair ends with a contest: one furnace, one hour, one pill each, judged by three old masters who have not smiled in twenty years.

ok.log: Your pill comes out round and green and smelling of rain. One of the old masters almost smiles.

fail.log: Your furnace cracks with a bang that makes the judges jump. Everyone remembers you, at least.

effects.log: You hand over herbs at the right moments. The young alchemist places third and bows to you.
Three furnaces crack; one pill glows. You write down what the glowing one did.

events.text: Everybody at the Hundred-Pill Fair is talking about a cloud-moss that grows on one cliff above the town and only blooms while the fair is on.

ok.log: You come down with a handful of blue moss and sell half of it before your feet touch the street.

fail.log: You get halfway, slip, and come down the quick way. Nothing is broken but your pride.

choices.text: Buy a little from a climber

effects.log: It costs 40 taels and it smells like the sky. You brew it into a tea that clears your head.

choices.text: Leave the cliff to the climbers

effects.log: Two climbers fall that week. You eat dumplings instead.

events.text: The plum rains drum on the roof of a great family's banquet hall. Every unmarried guest has been seated next to another unmarried guest, very much on purpose.

ok.log: You talk until the lanterns burn low. Whatever comes of it, it was a good evening.

fail.log: You spill the soup. Your neighbour laughs, which is something.

choices.text: Play the matchmaker for two shy guests

effects.log: You swap two place cards. By the last course the shy ones are not shy any more.
You stand under the eaves and listen to the plum rain. It is the best part of the night.

events.text: An old matchmaker in the market ties red threads around the wrists of passers-by for luck in the plum rain season. She holds out a thread to you without asking.

effects.log: She ties it with a knot you have never seen. "There," she says. "Now it knows where to find you."

choices.text: Ask her to tie one for a friend

effects.log: She ties a second thread and gives it to you to pass on. Your friend laughs, and wears it.
She shrugs and ties it to the next wrist. The rain keeps falling.

events.text: On the last night of the plum rains, couples float paper boats with candles down the river. Someone you know only a little holds out a second boat to you.

effects.log: The two candles drift side by side all the way to the bend. Neither of you says much. Neither of you needs to.
Your candle goes round the bend by itself, still burning.

choices.text: Give your boat to a lonely child

effects.log: The child floats it and shouts every time it bobs. That is a good night too.

events.text: Every inn on the capital road is full of candidates for the examinations, reciting the classics under their breath. One of them has fallen asleep over the books and the candle is about to set the pages alight.

choices.text: Wake the candidate and study together

effects.log: You test each other until dawn. It turns out you know more than you thought.

choices.text: Move the candle and let them sleep

effects.log: In the morning the candidate finds the pages whole and a cup of tea beside them, and never learns who.
There is no quieter inn. You sleep in a stable and dream of essays.

events.text: During the examination season the teahouses hold poetry contests on the theme the examiners chose last year: "the moon in a well". The prize is a fine brush.

ok.log: Your four lines make the teahouse go quiet. The brush is yours, and so, for a week, is the town's respect.

fail.log: Your poem rhymes "well" with "well". The teahouse is kind about it.

effects.log: You pick the shyest poet's poem. The shy poet will remember you all their life.
Forty poems about the moon in a well. Three of them are very good.

events.text: The examination lists go up on the palace wall at dawn. A crowd surges forward, and in the crush an old candidate who has failed eleven times cannot get close enough to read.

choices.text: Read the list for the old candidate

effects.log: You find the name in the third column. The old candidate sits down on the cobbles and laughs and laughs.

choices.text: Push to the front for yourself

effects.log: You read every name on the wall. Some of them you will meet again at court.
Joy, grief, disbelief. You learn more about people in an hour than in a year.

events.text: The Great Autumn Hunt opens the old hunting grounds. On the first morning a spirit boar as big as an ox comes crashing out of the red leaves straight at the hunting party.

ok.log: You turn it with one blow and it crashes off into the trees, beaten and alive. The hunters cheer you all the way home.

fail.log: It goes over you like a cart and keeps going. You get up eventually. Everyone is very polite about it.

choices.text: Pull a fallen hunter out of the way

effects.log: You drag a young hunter out of the boar's path by the collar. The hunter's family sends you a ham.
From the tree you have an excellent view of the boar, the hunters and the dust.

events.text: Tracks in the frost at the edge of the hunting grounds: something with five toes, each as wide as a hand, walked past the camp in the night and did not stop.

ok.log: At a frozen pool you see it: a white ape, watching you. It lets you look, and then it is gone. You will never forget it.

fail.log: The tracks vanish on bare rock. You are back at camp by dark, cold and curious.

choices.text: Warn the camp and double the watch

effects.log: Nobody sleeps much, but nobody is lost. In the morning the tracks have gone round the camp, twice.

choices.text: Pretend you did not see them

effects.log: You go back to bed. Something breathes outside the tent all night. You are almost sure.

events.text: The Great Autumn Hunt ends with a feast under the maples. The hunters argue about who should carry the hunt's banner next year, and somebody says your name.

effects.log: They tie the banner to your back and pour wine over your head. It is an honour, apparently.

choices.text: Say it should go to the oldest hunter

effects.log: The oldest hunter takes the banner with shaking hands and will not let go of it all night.
Your story about the boar gets bigger every time. By midnight it is a dragon.

events.text: The mists of the Sealed Valley part for the first time in a hundred years. Cultivators gather at the mouth of the valley, and nobody wants to be the first one in.

ok.log: Ten steps in, the air turns sweet and full of qi. You come out at dusk carrying a stone that hums.

fail.log: The mist turns you round three times and puts you back where you started, very dizzy.

effects.log: Six of you go in roped together and come out with six stories that do not agree.

choices.text: Wait and see who comes out

effects.log: Everyone comes out, eventually. Some of them are quieter than before.

events.text: Deep in the Sealed Valley a stone stele stands in a clearing, carved with a sword form so old the edges of the strokes have been worn round by rain.

choices.text: Study the form until night falls

ok.log: In the last light the worn strokes line up, and for one moment you see the form as its maker did.

fail.log: You stare until your eyes ache. The form keeps its secret, but your patience grows.

effects.log: You press paper to the stone and come away with the form in your bag. It will keep.
You walk on. Behind you somebody else sits down in front of the stele.

events.text: The mists of the Sealed Valley begin to close again. A cultivator you passed on the way in is still inside, calling for help from somewhere in the white.

ok.log: You find them by their voice and drag them out as the mist seals behind you. They owe you their life, and they say so.

fail.log: You both come out half frozen and very lost, but you come out.

choices.text: Light a fire at the mouth to guide them

effects.log: The cultivator walks out of the mist towards your fire just before it seals. Neither of you says much.

choices.text: Leave before the mist takes you too

effects.log: You leave. You do not find out what happened, and you try not to wonder.

events.text: The great caravans have come in from the west, and the market is full of silk, jade, glass and spices nobody here has a name for. A merchant with a red beard offers you a share in the return journey for 200 taels.

ok.log: The caravan comes back at the end of the season heavier than it went. Your share is worth 450 taels.

fail.log: The caravan comes back late and light. You get 150 back and a very good story.

choices.text: Haggle for a single bolt of silk

effects.log: You haggle for an hour and get the silk for half. The merchant seems pleased, which worries you.
You spend a whole day looking. You learn the names of eleven new spices.

events.text: A caravan master needs one more guard for the desert leg of the Silk Road: thirty days of sand, wind and the chance of raiders. The pay is good.

ok.log: Raiders come once, at night. They leave faster than they came. The caravan master pays you double.

fail.log: The raiders get away with two camels and your pride. You still get paid.

choices.text: Teach the guards a few forms instead

effects.log: You drill the guards for three days. They are better for it, and they buy you dinner.
The bells of the caravan go off into the west. You listen until you cannot hear them.

events.text: An old storyteller from the caravans sits in the inn yard every night of the season, telling of cities of glass, kings of the far west and a sea of sand that sings.

effects.log: By the end of the season you know the road as if you had walked it.

choices.text: Trade a story of your own

ok.log: The storyteller listens with eyes closed and then asks if they may tell it on the road. Your story goes west.

fail.log: Your story is shorter than you thought. The storyteller is kind and buys you tea.

effects.log: The storyteller eats like someone who has walked a long way. Then tells you a story nobody else hears.

events.text: Two sects march past the town under their banners on their way to settle a feud a hundred years old. Each column stops to ask you which side you are on.

choices.text: Tell them both to make peace

ok.log: Somehow you get two elders to sit down at the same table. The feud is not over, but the battle is.

fail.log: Both columns laugh at you and march on. At least nobody is angry with you in particular.

choices.text: Bandage the wounded of both sides

effects.log: You work through the night after the battle. Neither banner thanks you, but the wounded do.

choices.text: Bar your door until it is over

effects.log: Three days of drums. On the fourth, silence. You open the door very carefully.

events.text: After a battle of the War of Sect Banners you find a sect banner trampled into the mud by the river, and a wounded young disciple trying to drag it home.

choices.text: Carry the banner and the disciple home

effects.log: The sect at the top of the mountain bows to you as one. The banner is washed and hung again by evening.
The disciple is alive and furious about the banner. The sect forgives you; the disciple, eventually.

choices.text: Point the disciple to the road

effects.log: The disciple limps off with the banner over one shoulder. It is heavier than it looks.

events.text: In the War of Sect Banners, two champions are to duel at the river ford to decide a quarrel. One of them falls ill on the morning, and their sect asks you to stand in.

ok.log: The duel is short and clean. The quarrel is decided, and two sects know your name.

fail.log: You lose, but well. The sect that asked you still sends you a jar of wine and a letter of thanks.

effects.log: The physician gets the champion on their feet by noon. The duel goes ahead without you.

choices.text: Refuse: it is not your quarrel

effects.log: They find someone else. You hear later that it was close.

events.text: In the Season of Ancestors the lamps in every ancestral hall burn all night. An old caretaker is struggling to keep the lamps of a hall whose family has died out.

choices.text: Keep the lamps with the caretaker

effects.log: You trim wicks until dawn. The caretaker tells you the names on every tablet, and now somebody else knows them.
Thirty taels of oil. The hall stays bright until the season ends.

choices.text: Light one lamp and go home

effects.log: One lamp among a hundred dark ones. It is still a lamp.

events.text: In the Season of Ancestors the old ones of the town gather in the square to tell what their grandparents did. They look at you expectantly: what did yours do?

choices.text: Tell what you know of your forebears

effects.log: You tell it as well as you can. An old woman nods all the way through, as if she knew them.

choices.text: Tell of your own deeds instead

ok.log: You make it a good story. One day, someone says, the grandchildren will tell it.

fail.log: You get the dates wrong and the old ones correct you, kindly.

effects.log: You hear of a flood, a famine and a wedding that lasted nine days.

events.text: On the last night of the Season of Ancestors you find an old grave on the hillside with no name on it, and fresh offerings left in front of it by someone who did not stay.

choices.text: Leave an offering of your own

effects.log: You leave rice and a little wine. On the way down you meet nobody, and feel watched kindly.

choices.text: Clean the grave and set the stones straight

effects.log: It takes an hour. When you are done the grave looks like someone loved its owner.

choices.text: Wonder who it was, and walk on

effects.log: You never find out. Some graves keep their names to themselves.

events.text: In the Season of Falling Stars the sky over the sacred mountains is full of streaks of light every night. One of them seems to fall very close.

ok.log: In a smoking crater the size of a bowl lies a black stone, still warm. Your qi leaps toward it.

fail.log: You find a burnt tree and a very surprised owl, but no star.

effects.log: Every star that falls takes a little of your confusion with it.
You make one, and do not tell anyone.

events.text: An old astrologer has set up a bronze armillary on a hill and is charting the falling stars of the season. The astrologer says one of them is yours, and offers to show you which.

ok.log: You follow the bronze rings to one small star, and understand something about your own road.

fail.log: You see a great many stars and none of them in particular. The astrologer is patient.

choices.text: Help chart the falls all night

effects.log: By dawn the chart has three hundred marks on it, and your hand made half of them.

choices.text: Ask the astrologer about the astrologer

effects.log: The astrologer laughs. Nobody has asked in forty years. You hear a whole life before dawn.

events.text: A smith in the mountain town is trying to forge a blade from star iron that fell this season, and the metal will not take the hammer. The smith asks for a cultivator's qi to soften it.

choices.text: Pour your qi into the iron

ok.log: The star iron glows blue and folds like dough. The smith forges a blade and names it after you.

fail.log: The iron drinks your qi and stays as hard as ever. You are very tired, and a little wiser.

choices.text: Hold the tongs for the smith

effects.log: Hours of heat and noise. The blade is not finished, but the smith says it is closer.

choices.text: Tell the smith to let the iron rest

effects.log: The smith grumbles and puts it away. Some things fall from the sky to be left alone.
